narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which

scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Eagle's Dance: Inside the Circassian Djegu.
This is Circassian dance. Historical to present.
on_screen: Hero video, first 10 seconds (ua95fPR6HC8)
Title card: Circassian dance · Russia (North Caucasus), Turkey, Jordan, Israel · Historical to present

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Originating in the North Caucasus, these dances reflect the martial history and Nart Epic mythology of the Circassian people.
Historically, they served as physical training and social etiquette, with competition styles like Islamey used to demonstrate character and endurance.
on_screen: Map: Russia (North Caucasus), Turkey, Jordan, Israel · Central Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Dances are performed at weddings, social gatherings, and festivals.
They serve as a medium for courtship, social standing, and the preservation of cultural identity in the diaspora.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dances are divided into Wuj (circle), Qafa (partner), and Islamey (fast-paced).
Men dance on their toes with hands often behind their backs; women glide with motionless upper bodies.
Partners maintain a respectful distance, especially in Qafa, where touching is prohibited.
Watch for Zakladka, Qafa step.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (ua95fPR6HC8)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Counter-clockwise circles; pairs maintaining respectful distance.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is led by the pshine (accordion), accompanied by pkhachich (wood blocks), bereban (drum), and the shichepshin (fiddle).
Rhythms are often in 4/4 or 8/4 time, with specific pieces like Sheshen using off-beat bellows-pulling techniques.
Listen for the pshine (accordion), pkhachich (wood blocks), bereban (drum), pkhetaw (wooden table).
The pulse is 4/4 and 8/4.
Accordion-led melodies with sharp, rhythmic percussion from wood blocks and drums, creating a driving, disciplined sound.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Listen later: Narodnie pesni i instrumentalnie naigrishi adigov — Various
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: 1&2..3&4 for Tlleperush; off-beat rhythms for Sheshen.

narration: Before we go, one step. Qafa step: A smooth, gliding movement on the half-toes.
Wuj movement: Rhythmic foot stomping in a circle.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright, disciplined, and restrained; men often hold hands behind the back.
Women: open arms at slight angles, delicate fingertips. Men: folded at right angles or behind the back.
Motionless upper body for women; controlled, austere torso for men.
